key_insight: Wave breaking changes the usual shoaling-driven rogue-wave amplification: near a steep breakwater, nonlinearity first raises extreme-wave likelihood but then reduces it as breaking becomes dominant.
engineering_relevance: For coastal design and hazard assessment, steep-bottom geometry can sustain large excess kurtosis and elevated extreme-wave risk near the breakwater crest, so breaking effects must be included in nearshore predictions.
method: Model irregular waves over a submerged symmetric breakwater using fully nonlinear energetics.
Include wave-breaking effects via a height-to-depth proxy, WKB wavenumber variation, and slope-corrected mild-slope refraction.
Validate the theory with 30 m wave-flume experiments on broad-banded unidirectional waves over a 1/5 slope breakwater.
evidence_signal: The flume measurements show elevated excess kurtosis persists near the breaking limit and reaches a maximum at least four times larger than in other ocean processes, peaking over the breakwater and about half a deep-water wavelength shoreward of the shoal.
watch_item: The conclusions are geometry- and slope-dependent, so results from the steep 1/5 breakwater may not transfer directly to milder coastal slopes or fully 2D sea states.
paper_title: Energetics and Stochastics of Extreme Waves Breaking over a Symmetrical Breakwater
